title: Position and Direction for Grade 1: Positional Words for Kids + Free Quiz
meta_title: Position and Direction Grade 1 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach position and direction to Grade 1 with everyday positional words for kids: above, below, left, right, inside and near, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Above, below, left, right, inside, behind — the words a six-year-old uses to say where a thing is. Here is how positional language actually clicks for Grade 1, why left and right take years, and games to practise, with a quick quiz at the end.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 1 child where her water bottle is and you will rarely get a wrong answer — ‘under the bench’, ‘behind my bag’, ‘near the door’. Children already know where things are. What position and direction work in Grade 1 really teaches is the words for it, and one quiet idea underneath them all: a position only makes sense next to something else. ‘Above’ means above what? The bottle is under the bench, but it is also on the floor and next to a shoe. Same object, three true answers, depending on what you compare it to.

That is the whole subject in one sentence, and it is worth saying out loud to a six-year-old. Below are the positional words a Grade 1 child meets, the one pairing that genuinely takes years to settle (left and right), and the household games that teach all of it without a single worksheet — though there is a printable one at the end when you want written practice.

The positional words a Grade 1 child needs

NCERT and most Grade 1 syllabi cover the same small set of positional words for kids. None of them are hard on their own. The skill is using the right one and understanding that it always points at a reference object.

WordWhat it meansEveryday example
Above / belowHigher or lower than somethingThe fan is above the bed; the slippers are below it
On / underResting on top of, or beneathThe book is on the table; the cat is under it
Inside / outsideWithin a boundary, or out of itPencils inside the box, eraser outside it
In front of / behindAhead of, or at the back ofRiya stands in front of Aarav; Aarav is behind her
Near / farClose by, or a long way offThe shop is near; the school is far
Top / middle / bottomWhich of three levelsRice on the top shelf, dal in the middle, oil at the bottom
Up / downDirection of movementWe go up the stairs and down the slide
Left / rightThe two sides of the bodySpoon in the right hand, plate to the left

Position is always relative — teach that first

Here is the counter-intuitive bit that trips up even good lessons. We ask ‘Is the ball above or below?’ as if the ball has a fixed answer. It does not. The ball is above the floor and below the shelf at the very same moment. If a child says ‘below’ and you meant ‘above the floor’, she is not wrong — you forgot to name the reference.

So the fix is a habit: always say the second thing. Not ‘where is the cup?’ but ‘is the cup above or below the plate?’ Once children hear the reference object named every time, they start naming it themselves, and that is exactly the thinking you want. In my experience with six-year-olds, the ones who say ‘behind the door’ rather than just ‘behind’ are the ones who have really understood position.

Left and right: the honest truth

Every other word on the list settles within a few weeks. Left and right do not, and no amount of drilling in Grade 1 changes that. This is normal — the brain machinery for reliable left–right takes years, and plenty of adults still pause before saying which way to turn.

Why it is genuinely harder

Above and below are anchored to the world: the sky is up whichever way you face. Left and right are anchored to you, and they flip when you turn around. Worse, when you face another person their left is on your right. Ask two children to sit opposite each other and raise their right hands — the hands go up on opposite sides, and the confusion on their faces is the lesson. Mirror-image left–right is a skill that keeps maturing well past Grade 1, so do not treat a mix-up as a failure.

What actually helps

  • Give the correct hand a job the child cares about — the writing hand, the eating hand. A body memory beats a rule.
  • Use a permanent marker dot or a thread on one wrist for a week as a reference they can glance at.
  • Practise left and right that stay put (your own hands, your own sides) long before the mirror version (facing someone else).
  • Keep it low-stakes. ‘Other one’ said cheerfully teaches better than a frown.

Everyday games that teach position and direction

Positional language is the rare maths topic you can teach entirely without paper, and honestly you should for the first few weeks. It sticks far better when it is attached to real objects a child can touch and move.

  • Simon Says, position edition. ‘Put your hand above your head’, ‘stand behind the chair’, ‘keep the spoon inside the cup’. Fast, funny, and it forces the child to act out the word.
  • Toy on a chair. Give one instruction at a time — on it, under it, in front of it, behind it, next to it. Then swap and let the child give you the instructions; explaining is where understanding shows.
  • Treasure directions. Hide a small toy and guide with words only: ‘go near the almirah, look on the bottom shelf, behind the box.’ This chains several words into one journey.
  • Kitchen shelf sorting. Top, middle, bottom become real when a child decides which shelf the dal tin goes on. Everyday chores are free maths practice.
  • Follow the map arrows. Draw simple up, down, left, right arrows on paper and have the child walk the path. This bridges positional words into early direction.

What good progress looks like by the end of Grade 1

By year end, aim for a child who uses above, below, inside, outside, near, far, in front of, behind, and top–middle–bottom accurately and, crucially, names the reference object without being reminded. Up and down should be automatic. Left and right will be right most of the time for their own body, wobbly when facing someone else — and that is exactly on track, not behind. Push understanding, not speed.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz built on clear word-pictures — no images needed, just read each scene and pick the answer — covering above and below, left and right, inside, behind and near and far. Let your child talk through each one aloud; the reasoning matters more than the tick. When you want written practice with pictures to circle and colour, the printable Grade 1 position and direction worksheet at the end gives graded pages with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Position and Direction Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on positional words — above, below, left, right, inside, behind and near. Read each scene, pick an answer, then press Check my score.

questions.q: A cat is sitting on top of a table. Where is the cat compared to the table?
questions.explanation: Sitting on top means the cat is higher than the table, so it is above it.

questions.q: Riya stands in the queue. Aarav is right behind her. Who is in front?
questions.explanation: If Aarav is behind Riya, then Riya is the one in front of Aarav.

questions.q: A pencil is kept inside the pencil box. Where is the pencil?
questions.explanation: Inside means within the boundary of the box, so the pencil is inside it.

questions.q: You hold a spoon in your right hand and a plate is on your other side. Which side is the plate on?
questions.explanation: The spoon is in the right hand, so the other side is the left. The plate is on the left.

questions.q: The fan is on the ceiling and the bed is on the floor. Where is the fan compared to the bed?
questions.explanation: The ceiling is higher than the floor, so the fan is above the bed.

questions.q: The market is a two-minute walk away. The airport is many hours away. Which one is far?
questions.explanation: Two minutes away is near; many hours away is far. The airport is far.

questions.q: On a shelf, rice is at the top, dal is in the middle, oil is at the bottom. Where is the dal?
questions.explanation: Between the top rice and the bottom oil, the dal sits in the middle level.

questions.q: A ball is on the floor, a shelf is high on the wall. Which word describes the ball next to the shelf?
questions.explanation: The floor is lower than a high shelf, so the ball is below the shelf.

faq.q: What positional words should a Grade 1 child know?
faq.a: The core set is above and below, on and under, inside and outside, in front of and behind, near and far, top-middle-bottom, up and down, and left and right. All except left and right usually settle within a few weeks.

faq.q: Why does my child mix up left and right?
faq.a: Because left and right are tied to the body and flip when you turn around — unlike up and above, which stay fixed to the world. Mirror-image left and right keeps maturing for years, so mix-ups in Grade 1 are completely normal, not a problem.

faq.q: Do I need worksheets to teach position and direction?
faq.a: Not at first. For the early weeks, real objects work better — a toy on a chair, Simon Says, sorting kitchen shelves. Move to written practice once the words are secure in speech.

faq.q: How do I explain that position is relative?
faq.a: Always name the second thing. Instead of asking ‘where is the cup?’ ask ‘is the cup above or below the plate?’ The same object can be above one thing and below another at once, so the reference object is what makes an answer true.
